This exercise reworks [Hands-on Exercise 7](../../Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex07/Hands-on_Ex07.qmd)
with the [`catchment`](https://uva-bi-sdad.github.io/catchment/) package, one of the R
resources listed for Lesson 7. It uses the same data and the same data preparation. No
in-class script for this lesson has been published, so the choice of models and checks
below is my own.

## 1. Overview

Hands-on Exercise 7 computed Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM accessibility to eldercare with
`SpatialAcc`. That package returns one number per hexagon and nothing else.

`catchment`, from the University of Virginia's Biocomplexity Institute, covers the
floating catchment area (FCA) family with one function, `catchment_ratio()`, and three
things about it make it worth a second pass over the same data:

- the shape of the catchment is a single argument, so 2SFCA, E2SFCA, KD2SFCA and 3SFCA
  differ only in what is passed to `weight`;
- besides each hexagon's accessibility it can return the **demand each centre faces**,
  which is the first step of every FCA model and the part `SpatialAcc` hides;
- it lines up the cost matrix with demand and supply **by ID**, not by position.

All FCA models answer the same question in two steps. First, each centre's capacity is
divided by the demand within its catchment, giving a supply-to-demand ratio. Second,
each hexagon adds up the ratios of the centres whose catchments it falls in. The
variants differ in how a catchment's edge is drawn.

## 2. Getting Started

`catchment` is not on CRAN. It installs from GitHub:

```{r}
#| eval: false
remotes::install_github("uva-bi-sdad/catchment")
```

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, tmap,
               SpatialAcc, catchment)
```

`SpatialAcc` is loaded only to check that `catchment` reproduces Hands-on Exercise 7.

## 3. Data Preparation

The data and every preparation step are the same as in Hands-on Exercise 7: URA's 2014
subzones, 3,125 hexagons of 250 m radius, 120 eldercare centres, and the road distance
from every hexagon to every centre.

### 3.1 Importing the geospatial data

```{r}
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")
```

```{r}
hexagons <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "hexagons")
```

```{r}
eldercare <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "ELDERCARE")
```

### 3.2 Updating the CRS

```{r}
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414)
hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414)

c(mpsz = st_crs(mpsz)$epsg,
  hexagons = st_crs(hexagons)$epsg,
  eldercare = st_crs(eldercare)$epsg)
```

### 3.3 Cleaning the attribute fields

```{r}
eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)

hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)
```

As before, a constant 100 stands in for real demand and capacity.

### 3.4 Importing and checking the distance matrix

```{r}
ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)
```

```{r}
od_check <- ODMatrix %>%
  group_by(origin_id) %>%
  summarise(spread_m = max(total_cost) - min(total_cost),
            nearest_m = min(total_cost))

c(origins = nrow(od_check),
  same_distance_to_every_centre = sum(od_check$spread_m == 0))
```

These are the `r sum(od_check$spread_m == 0)` hexagons that Hands-on Exercise 7 found
with one distance repeated for all 120 centres, which no road network produces. Section
3.6 deals with them.

### 3.5 Tidying the distance matrix

```{r}
distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = destination_id,
              values_from = total_cost)

c(rows_match_hexagons = identical(distmat$origin_id,
                                  as.numeric(hexagons$fid)),
  cols_match_eldercare = identical(as.numeric(names(distmat)[-1]),
                                   as.numeric(eldercare$fid)))
```

```{r}
distmat <- distmat %>%
  select(-origin_id)

distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat / 1000)
```

That is where Hands-on Exercise 7's preparation ends. `catchment` needs one more thing:
the matrix's rows and columns named with the hexagon and centre IDs, so that it can
match them to demand and supply by name. The column names are already the centre IDs;
the row names come from the order `pivot_wider()` used, which is the order origins first
appear in the CSV.

```{r}
rownames(distmat_km) <- ODMatrix %>% distinct(origin_id) %>% pull(origin_id)

dim(distmat_km)
distmat_km[1:3, 1:5]
```

### 3.6 A clean copy of the matrix

`catchment` treats a missing cost as "no connection". I keep `distmat_km` intact for the
comparison with Hands-on Exercise 7, and make a second copy in which the repeated rows
are set to missing, so those hexagons neither claim nor compete for any centre.

```{r}
flat_ids <- od_check$origin_id[od_check$spread_m == 0]

cost_km <- distmat_km
cost_km[as.character(flat_ids), ] <- NA

c(rows_set_missing = sum(rowSums(is.na(cost_km)) == ncol(cost_km)))
```

### 3.7 Demand and supply tables

`catchment_ratio()` accepts plain vectors, but data frames with an ID column let it align
everything by name. The default column names it looks for are `GEOID` and `count`.

```{r}
consumers <- hexagons %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(GEOID = as.character(fid), count = demand)

providers <- eldercare %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(GEOID = as.character(fid), count = capacity)
```

## 4. Reproducing Hands-on Exercise 7 First

Before trusting a new package, I check it against the old one. `SpatialAcc`'s KD2SFCA
weights a centre at distance *d* by `exp(-d^2)` and drops it beyond `d0`. `catchment`'s
Gaussian weight is `exp(-d^2 / (2 * scale^2))`. The two are the same function when
`2 * scale^2 = 1`, that is `scale = 1 / sqrt(2)`, and `catchment`'s `max_cost` plays the
part of `d0`.

```{r}
kd_spatialacc <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km,
                    d0 = 5, power = 2, family = "KD2SFCA")

kd_catchment <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, distmat_km,
                                weight = "gaussian", scale = 1 / sqrt(2),
                                max_cost = 5)

twosfca_spatialacc <- ac(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km,
                         d0 = 5, family = "2SFCA")

twosfca_catchment <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, distmat_km,
                                     weight = 5)

c(KD2SFCA_max_abs_difference = max(abs(kd_spatialacc - kd_catchment)),
  `2SFCA_max_abs_difference` = max(abs(twosfca_spatialacc - twosfca_catchment)))
```

Both agree to floating-point precision. This matters beyond reassurance: it pins down
that the two packages express the same kernel with different parameters. A `scale` of 5
in `catchment` would not mean what a `d0` of 5 means in `SpatialAcc`, and copying
numbers between them without this check would silently change the model.

## 5. Four Models on the Same Data

From here on I use the clean matrix `cost_km`. The four models differ only in `weight`:

| Model | `weight` | Catchment |
|---|---|---|
| 2SFCA | `5` | everyone within 5 km counts fully, no one beyond |
| E2SFCA | `list(c(1.5, 1), c(3, 0.68), c(5, 0.22))` | steps: full weight to 1.5 km, 0.68 to 3 km, 0.22 to 5 km |
| KD2SFCA | `"gaussian"`, `scale = 1/sqrt(2)`, `max_cost = 5` | smooth decay, as in Hands-on Exercise 7 |
| 3SFCA | as KD2SFCA, plus `normalize_weight = TRUE` | a hexagon's demand is shared out among the centres it can reach |

The E2SFCA step weights 1, 0.68 and 0.22 are the ones Luo and Qi (2009) used for 10, 20
and 30-minute drive zones. Placing their edges at 1.5, 3 and 5 km is my choice, made so
that the outer edge matches the 5 km catchment of the other models.

```{r}
fca <- hexagons %>%
  mutate(
    `2SFCA` = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                              weight = 5),
    E2SFCA = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                             weight = list(c(1.5, 1), c(3, 0.68), c(5, 0.22))),
    KD2SFCA = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                              weight = "gaussian", scale = 1 / sqrt(2),
                              max_cost = 5),
    `3SFCA` = catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                              weight = "gaussian", scale = 1 / sqrt(2),
                              max_cost = 5, normalize_weight = TRUE),
    flat = fid %in% flat_ids)
```

`catchment` gives the masked hexagons a score of 0, as if they had no centre in range.
That is not what we know about them: their distances are unknown, not long. So I
record them as missing.

```{r}
models <- c("2SFCA", "E2SFCA", "KD2SFCA", "3SFCA")

fca <- fca %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(models), ~ if_else(flat, NA_real_, .x)))

fca %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(models), names_to = "model") %>%
  group_by(model = factor(model, levels = models)) %>%
  summarise(zero = sum(value == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            missing = sum(is.na(value)),
            median = signif(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            max = signif(max(value, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            places_allocated = sum(value * 100, na.rm = TRUE))
```

The scores are in places per unit of demand: with 100 places per centre and 100 units
of demand per hexagon, a 2SFCA score of 0.1 means the hexagon can draw on 0.1 places for
each unit of its demand. Every model gives zero to the same hexagons, the ones with no
centre within 5 km. The last column is the subject of section 7.1.

```{r}
fca %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!flat) %>%
  mutate(nearest_km = apply(cost_km[as.character(fid), ], 1, min)) %>%
  select(all_of(models), nearest_km) %>%
  cor(method = "spearman") %>%
  round(3)
```

The step and kernel versions sit between plain 2SFCA and distance to the nearest
centre: the more a model discounts the far edge of the catchment, the more its ranking
looks like a ranking by nearest distance. 3SFCA barely reorders KD2SFCA (rank
correlation `r round(cor(fca$KD2SFCA, fca[["3SFCA"]], method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"), 3)`),
because with equal demand everywhere, sharing a hexagon's demand among its centres
changes the levels much more than the order.

## 6. Mapping the Four Models

Hands-on Exercise 7's KD2SFCA map used ten quantile classes, and with 41% of hexagons
tied at zero the classes collapsed and drew "no access" in mid-blue. Here all four models
share one set of breaks, zero gets its own grey class, and the masked hexagons are shown
as missing.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7.5
fca_long <- fca %>%
  select(fid, all_of(models)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(models), names_to = "model", values_to = "access") %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = models))

# tmap facets every layer, so the centres need one copy per model
eldercare_long <- map_dfr(models, ~ mutate(eldercare,
                                           model = factor(.x, levels = models)))

tm_shape(fca_long) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "access",
              col = NA,
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 1e-9, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 2),
                labels = c("0, no centre within 5 km", "under 0.001",
                           "0.001 to 0.01", "0.01 to 0.05", "0.05 to 0.1",
                           "0.1 to 0.2", "0.2 and above"),
                values = c("grey85", "#deebf7", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1",
                           "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c"),
                value.na = "white",
                label.na = "no valid distance"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Places per unit of demand")) +
  tm_shape(eldercare_long) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "red") +
  tm_facets_wrap(by = "model", ncols = 2) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```

The four maps agree on where access is zero, since that depends only on the 5 km edge.
Inside the catchments, 2SFCA is the flattest, because every centre within 5 km counts
in full; the kernel models concentrate access close to the centres.

## 7. What `catchment` Shows That `SpatialAcc` Does Not

### 7.1 Every model hands out exactly 12,000 places

The `places_allocated` column in section 5 is 12,000 for every model, which is the
total capacity of 120 centres with 100 places each. That is not a coincidence. With
$P_i$ the demand of hexagon $i$, $S_j$ the capacity of centre $j$ and $W_{ij}$ the
catchment weight, an FCA score is

$$A_i = \sum_j W_{ij} R_j, \qquad R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_k P_k W_{kj}},$$

so the demand-weighted total is

$$\sum_i P_i A_i = \sum_j R_j \sum_i P_i W_{ij} = \sum_j S_j.$$

Whatever the weights, each centre's capacity is shared out once among the demand in its
catchment, as long as every centre has some demand within reach (here every centre
does). This is what makes FCA scores interpretable in a way Hansen's are not: added up
over any area, they give the number of places that area can draw on. Section 8 uses
this.

### 7.2 2SFCA counts each hexagon's demand many times over

`return_type = "demand"` returns the first step of the model: the demand each centre
faces. Under 2SFCA a hexagon within 5 km of ten centres is counted, in full, in all ten
catchments. Normalising the weights, the "3" in 3SFCA, splits it among them instead.
With binary weights the effect can be counted exactly.

```{r}
demand_2sfca <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                                weight = 5, return_type = "demand")

demand_3sfca <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers, cost_km,
                                weight = 5, normalize_weight = TRUE,
                                return_type = "demand")

centres_in_range <- rowSums(cost_km < 5, na.rm = TRUE)

c(actual_demand_within_5km = 100 * sum(centres_in_range > 0),
  demand_counted_by_2SFCA = sum(demand_2sfca),
  demand_counted_by_3SFCA = sum(demand_3sfca),
  mean_centres_within_5km = round(mean(centres_in_range[centres_in_range > 0]), 1))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## 2SFCA inflates demand by a factor of `r round(sum(demand_2sfca) / (100 * sum(centres_in_range > 0)), 1)`

The hexagons within 5 km of a centre hold `r format(100 * sum(centres_in_range > 0), big.mark = ",")`
units of demand. 2SFCA counts `r format(sum(demand_2sfca), big.mark = ",")`, because the
average hexagon in range is within 5 km of
`r round(mean(centres_in_range[centres_in_range > 0]), 1)` centres and is counted in
every one of their catchments. 3SFCA's normalised weights count each hexagon once, and
the total comes back to exactly `r format(sum(demand_3sfca), big.mark = ",")`.

This is the demand inflation that Páez, Higgins and Vivona (2019) describe. Section 7.1
showed that the total *supply* still balances, so the inflation does not change the
island-wide sum. What it changes is which centres look crowded.
:::

```{r}
crowding <- eldercare %>%
  st_join(mpsz %>% select(PLN_AREA_N)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(fid, PLN_AREA_N,
            demand_2SFCA = demand_2sfca,
            demand_3SFCA = round(demand_3sfca),
            rank_2SFCA = min_rank(desc(demand_2sfca)),
            rank_3SFCA = min_rank(desc(demand_3sfca)))

crowding %>% arrange(rank_2SFCA) %>% head(5)
crowding %>% arrange(rank_3SFCA) %>% head(5)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
top5_2 <- crowding %>% arrange(rank_2SFCA) %>% head(5)
top5_3 <- crowding %>% arrange(rank_3SFCA) %>% head(5)
```

The two models disagree about which centres are under the most pressure. Under 2SFCA,
the most crowded centres are in `r paste(unique(top5_2$PLN_AREA_N), collapse = ", ")`:
central estates where many centres sit close together, so every hexagon nearby is
counted by all of them. Under 3SFCA those hexagons are shared, and the most crowded
centres are instead in `r paste(unique(top5_3$PLN_AREA_N), collapse = ", ")`, where a
centre is the only option for a large surrounding area. The rank correlation between
the two crowding measures across all 120 centres is
`r round(cor(crowding$demand_2SFCA, crowding$demand_3SFCA, method = "spearman"), 2)`.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
crowding_sf <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  left_join(crowding, by = "fid") %>%
  mutate(`2SFCA` = 100 * demand_2SFCA / sum(demand_2SFCA),
         `3SFCA` = 100 * demand_3SFCA / sum(demand_3SFCA)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(`2SFCA`, `3SFCA`),
               names_to = "model", values_to = "share")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "grey96", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = crowding_sf, aes(size = share),
          shape = 21, fill = "#137C8B", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7, name = "Share of all\ndemand counted (%)") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  theme_void()
```

For a planner deciding where to add places, this is the difference between expanding in
Toa Payoh and expanding in Yishun. Neither answer is trustworthy with constant demand,
but the exercise shows that the choice of model, not just the data, decides it.

### 7.3 Alignment by ID

Hands-on Exercise 7 noted that `SpatialAcc::ac()` pairs the matrix with demand and
supply purely by position, which is harmless here only because capacity is constant. To
see what ID alignment buys, I give the centres different capacities and shuffle their
order.

```{r}
set.seed(626)
providers_varied <- providers %>%
  mutate(count = sample(50:150, n(), replace = TRUE))

shuffled <- providers_varied %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 1)

reference <- catchment_ratio(consumers, providers_varied, cost_km, weight = 5)
by_id <- catchment_ratio(consumers, shuffled, cost_km, weight = 5)
by_position <- catchment_ratio(consumers$count, shuffled$count, cost_km, weight = 5)

c(data_frames_match_reference = isTRUE(all.equal(by_id, reference)),
  plain_vectors_match_reference = isTRUE(all.equal(by_position, reference)))
```

Passed as data frames, the shuffled centres are matched to their columns by ID and the
result is unchanged. Passed as plain vectors, the same shuffle silently gives every
centre another centre's capacity, and nothing warns about it. The safe habit is to
always pass `consumers` and `providers` as tables with IDs.

## 8. Regional Summary with `catchment_aggregate()`

Hands-on Exercise 7 compared regions with boxplots, and found that its `st_join()`
counted many hexagons several times. `catchment_aggregate()` does the comparison the FCA
way: it adds up `access × demand` over the hexagons in each region and divides by the
region's demand. I assign each hexagon to one region with `largest = TRUE` and give the
masked hexagons zero demand, so they drop out of both sums.

```{r}
hex_region <- st_join(hexagons, mpsz %>% select(REGION_N), largest = TRUE) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

region_map <- split(as.character(hex_region$fid), hex_region$REGION_N)
regions <- data.frame(GEOID = names(region_map))

aggregate_model <- function(model) {
  from <- fca %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    transmute(GEOID = as.character(fid),
              access = replace_na(.data[[model]], 0),
              population = if_else(flat, 0, demand))
  list(
    per_100 = 100 * catchment_aggregate(from, regions, map = region_map),
    places = catchment_aggregate(from, regions, map = region_map,
                                 return_type = "region"))
}

agg_2 <- aggregate_model("2SFCA")
agg_3 <- aggregate_model("3SFCA")

region_summary <- tibble(
  region = names(region_map),
  hexagons = lengths(region_map),
  places_per_100_2SFCA = round(agg_2$per_100[region], 2),
  share_of_places_2SFCA = round(100 * agg_2$places[region] / 12000, 1),
  share_of_places_3SFCA = round(100 * agg_3$places[region] / 12000, 1))

as.data.frame(region_summary)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
central <- region_summary %>% filter(region == "CENTRAL REGION")
west <- region_summary %>% filter(region == "WEST REGION")
```

Because the regions partition the island and FCA conserves supply, each share column
adds up to 100%: it is a split of the 12,000 places. Under 2SFCA the Central region,
with `r central$hexagons` of the 3,125 hexagons, can draw on
`r central$share_of_places_2SFCA`% of all places, and the West, with
`r west$hexagons` hexagons, on `r west$share_of_places_2SFCA`%. The regional shares
barely move between 2SFCA and 3SFCA, because sharing demand reshuffles pressure between
neighbouring centres more than between regions.

## 9. What I Take From This Exercise

**Reproduce before you extend.** `catchment` and `SpatialAcc` implement the same KD2SFCA
with different parameters (`scale = 1/sqrt(2)` against `power = 2`), and only an
explicit side-by-side run showed that they agree to floating-point precision. Without
that check I would have had no way to know whether a difference between the packages
was a modelling difference or a translation error.

**FCA scores are allocations, and that makes them auditable.** Every FCA model here
hands out exactly the 12,000 places in the system. That identity is a free test of any
implementation and is what allows regional totals to be read as shares of supply.
Hansen's potential has no such property.

**The choice between 2SFCA and 3SFCA changes the policy answer.** 2SFCA counts each
hexagon's demand in every catchment it touches, inflating total demand by a factor of
`r round(sum(demand_2sfca) / (100 * sum(centres_in_range > 0)), 1)`. That makes clustered
central centres look the most crowded; once demand is shared, the most pressured centres
are isolated ones in outer towns. Hexagon-level access barely changes, but the question
"where should places be added?" gets a different answer.

**Pass tables with IDs, never bare vectors.** `catchment` aligns by ID when it is given
IDs and by position when it is not. The second mode reproduces exactly the silent
misalignment risk of `SpatialAcc`.

**Missing is not zero.** `catchment` turns an unknown distance into "no connection", which
scores as zero access. For the 159 hexagons with defective distances that would have
reported unknown access as no access, so they are masked back to missing.

**What I would change.** The same as in Hands-on Exercise 7: real demand and capacity.
With resident counts aged 65 and over as demand and licensed places as capacity, the
2SFCA and 3SFCA crowding maps in section 7.2 would become a usable shortlist of centres
to expand, rather than a demonstration that the method decides the answer.

- Dai, D. (2010). Black residential segregation, disparities in spatial access to health care facilities, and late-stage breast cancer diagnosis in metropolitan Detroit. *Health & Place*, 16(5), 1038-1052.
- Wan, N., Zou, B. and Sternberg, T. (2012). A three-step floating catchment area method for analyzing spatial access to health services. *International Journal of Geographical Information Science*, 26(6), 1073-1089.
- Páez, A., Higgins, C. D. and Vivona, S. F. (2019). Demand and level of service inflation in floating catchment area (FCA) methods. *PLOS One*, 14(6), e0218773.
- Biocomplexity Institute, University of Virginia. *catchment: Calculate spatial access and availability metrics*, version 0.0.1. https://github.com/uva-bi-sdad/catchment
